claims.statement: The majority of animal cells are 10 to 20 micrometres in diameter and rarely vary more than twofold outside that band, and a published model of the human colonic crypt adopts a mean cell radius of 5 micrometres, giving a crypt cell of about 10 micrometres across.
claims.scope: A working order-of-magnitude figure for the width of a typical animal cell and of a colonic epithelial cell, used to compare cell size against instrument thresholds at college-intro level.
claims.uncertainty: The 10 to 20 micrometre band is a general statement about animal cells rather than a measurement of human colonic epithelium, and the 5 micrometre radius is a parameter chosen for a computational model rather than a reported morphometric result. A colonic epithelial cell is columnar and therefore taller than it is wide, so a single width does not describe it fully. Every conclusion in this lesson is stated so that it holds across the whole band.

claims.statement: Cell sizes across the human body vary over about seven orders of magnitude, from red blood cells to the largest muscle fibres, so no single value is the size of a human cell and any working figure is a band.
claims.scope: The spread of cell sizes across all human cell types, used to justify treating a cell width as an order-of-magnitude band rather than a constant.
claims.uncertainty: The seven-order range is quoted in mass rather than in diameter, and a mass ratio compresses to a smaller ratio in length. The lesson uses the statement only to establish that the spread is very wide.

claims.statement: The reference limit of human spatial vision behind the 20/20 standard is about 1 minute of arc, equivalent to 60 pixels per degree, while one study measured a mean high-contrast foveal achromatic threshold of about 94 pixels per degree; converting those angles at an ordinary viewing distance of 25 to 35 centimetres gives a smallest resolvable separation of roughly 0.05 to 0.1 millimetres within the lesson's model.
claims.scope: An order-of-magnitude threshold for the finest detail an unaided human eye separates at ordinary viewing distance, used to explain why cells could not be seen before lenses.
claims.uncertainty: The angular limit is the sourced quantity; the length is not, because an eye has no fixed length threshold. The conversion depends on the viewing distance assumed and on which angular figure is used, and those choices move the answer between roughly 0.05 and 0.1 millimetres. Acuity also varies between people, falls away from the fovea, and depends on contrast and illumination, none of which this lesson models.

claims.statement: The resolution limit of conventional light microscopy is about 250 nanometres in the lateral directions, and an object smaller than that limit appears at the size of the limit however much the image is enlarged, while two objects closer together than the limit are never separated into two.
claims.scope: The lateral resolution floor of conventional light microscopy, used to separate the concept of magnification from the concept of resolution and to place cells and molecules on opposite sides of an instrument threshold.
claims.uncertainty: The figure depends on wavelength and numerical aperture and is therefore a representative value rather than a constant. Super-resolution methods, which the source is actually about, defeat this limit by means the lesson does not teach, so the statement describes conventional light microscopy only.

claims.statement: The DNA double helix is about 2 nanometres, or 20 angstroms, across.
claims.scope: The width of the B-form double helix, used as the bottom rung of a scale ladder.
claims.uncertainty: The value is a round figure for the common B form; reported diameters vary somewhat with form and with the conditions the molecule is measured in. Nothing in the lesson depends on the value beyond its order of magnitude.

claims.statement: Robert Hooke's Micrographia, published in 1665, defined the term cell for a small chamber surrounded by walls; the cork he examined he did not classify as part of a plant, comparing it instead to a mushroom, and he separately recorded that cells in plants were filled with fluid.
claims.scope: The origin of the word cell in seventeenth-century microscopy, and what Hooke did and did not conclude from cork.
claims.uncertainty: Historians differ over how much of the popular account of this episode is accurate, and one of the two sources here exists to correct that account. The lesson therefore states only what both sources support and flags that the empty chambers of cork are dead tissue rather than a general picture of what a cell contains.

claims.statement: Cell theory was established in Berlin in 1838 and 1839, by Matthias Schleiden working on plants and Theodor Schwann on animals, postulating that all tissues are composed of cells as a basic unit. A historical three-part statement adds that cells carry the attributes of life and arise by division of pre-existing cells; the modern lineage principle is broader because specialised cells such as skeletal muscle fibres can form by fusion of pre-existing cells.
claims.scope: The content and dating of cell theory as a historical position, together with the modern cellular-lineage qualification needed for a first cell-biology lesson.
claims.uncertainty: The exact list of propositions differs between accounts, and historians emphasise different tenets. The division wording is retained only as a historical formulation; it is not presented as a universal formation mechanism for every specialised cell.

claims.statement: Being a living cell does not require an individual cell to remain able to divide; mature skeletal muscle fibres are living multinucleate cells formed by fusion of pre-existing myoblasts and do not themselves divide.
claims.scope: The boundary needed to keep the lesson's definition of a cell and its statement of cellular lineage from requiring reproductive capacity of every differentiated cell.
claims.uncertainty: Skeletal muscle is used as one clear boundary case. The lesson does not attempt to catalogue every postmitotic or multinucleate cell type.

claims.statement: In current scientific usage, a theory is a concise, coherent and predictive explanation for a broad range of phenomena that can integrate many hypotheses; hypotheses may be narrower explanations, the terminology varies between disciplines, and scientific knowledge remains open to revision when evidence warrants it.
claims.scope: The distinction among scientific theory, hypothesis and everyday guess used in this lesson, without treating the terms as a universal promotion ladder.
claims.uncertainty: Scientific fields do not use theory and hypothesis with perfect consistency. The lesson therefore describes their typical differences in breadth and explanatory role and makes evidence, scope and revisability more important than the label.

claims.statement: Rudolf Virchow's Cellularpathologie, first published in 1858, established the concept that diseases can be diagnosed by analysing the cells in a patient's tissue, which is the basis of histological diagnosis today.
claims.scope: The historical origin of histological diagnosis as a general medical practice, used to show what cell theory licensed in medicine.
claims.uncertainty: This is a statement about the origin and general basis of a discipline. It carries no diagnostic criterion, no test performance, and nothing about how any particular specimen should be interpreted, and the lesson makes no such claim.

claims.statement: A crypt in the human descending colon holds approximately 700 cells, arranged about 32 along its length and about 22 around its circumference.
claims.scope: The cell population and cell-wise dimensions of a single crypt in the descending colon, used for renewal arithmetic and for placing a crypt on a scale ladder.
claims.uncertainty: The figure is for the descending colon and comes from a modelling study that assembled it from reported measurements; crypt size varies along the colon, between people, and with disease. The lesson uses it only to an order of magnitude and derives crypt length from it as an estimate rather than reading a measured length from the source.

claims.statement: A colonic crypt is an invagination of the epithelial lining whose base is the stem-cell niche; cells differentiate as they migrate upward and are fully differentiated at the crypt top, Wnt signalling decreases progressively up the crypt axis, colonocytes maintain the integrity of the epithelial barrier, and mucins secreted by goblet cells form the mucus layer that protects against pathogen invasion.
claims.scope: The layout of the colonic crypt, the direction of migration and differentiation, the decline of Wnt signalling along the crypt axis, and the barrier and mucus functions of the epithelium, at the level of detail a first lesson needs.
claims.uncertainty: The lesson omits the specific molecular signal and treats the gradient qualitatively; the mechanism by which a cell reads its position is the subject of a later lesson in this block and is not established here. The account describes the healthy adult human colon and is not a description of disease.

claims.statement: Continuous intestinal epithelial barrier function requires a contiguous cell layer and the junctions that seal the paracellular space, while epithelial cells also support transcellular transport through individual cells; continuous tissue-level exclusion, paracellular permeability and transcellular permeability are therefore related but distinct properties.
claims.scope: The distinction needed to classify continuous barrier coverage as an emergent tissue property without denying permeability and transport properties of individual epithelial cells.
claims.uncertainty: The lesson uses only the high-level distinction among transcellular, paracellular and continuous tissue-level properties. It does not teach molecular permeability pathways, disease mechanisms, measurement, or treatment.

claims.statement: The colonic epithelium renews itself every three to five days, with the absorptive enterocytes replaced every four to five days; a second, independent report gives the same three-to-five-day interval for replacement of the human intestinal epithelium.
claims.scope: The turnover interval of the healthy adult human colonic epithelium, used for renewal arithmetic and to motivate the emergence argument.
claims.uncertainty: Reported intervals differ between studies, between regions of the intestine, and between the cell types within one crypt; the same review notes that some enteroendocrine cells persist far longer than the enterocytes. The lesson treats the interval as a few days rather than as a precise value.

claims.statement: Cells in the lower half of the human colonic crypt migrate upward at an average speed of around 4 micrometres per hour.
claims.scope: The measured average upward migration speed in the lower half of a normal human colonic crypt, used as an independent consistency check on the renewal interval.
claims.uncertainty: The figure is reported for the lower half of the crypt only. Extending it over the whole climb to estimate a base-to-surface transit time assumes a speed that does not change with height, which the source does not report and which may be false. The lesson states that assumption where it makes the estimate.

claims.statement: Quantitative research on the normal and the neoplastic human colon is conducted at the level of the crypt and its cell populations, rather than by cataloguing single cells in isolation.
claims.scope: The level of biological organisation at which published colon research operates, used to connect the lesson's emergence argument to how the tissue is actually studied.
claims.uncertainty: This is an observation about two published works and the practice they represent, not a survey of the field, and it says nothing about routine diagnostic practice, criteria, or reporting. Single-cell methods are also used in colon research, and their existence does not conflict with the point being made about crypt-level organisation.

claims.statement: An adult human body holds cells of order 10 to the 13: about 3.0 x 10^13 by one estimate for a 70 kg reference man, and about 36 trillion for an adult male and 28 trillion for an adult female by a later independent estimate. The colon carries about 3.8 x 10^13 bacteria, which is the same order of magnitude as the body's own cell count.
claims.scope: Order-of-magnitude counts of human cells in a reference adult body and of bacteria in the colon, used to show what the epithelial sheet stands between.
claims.uncertainty: The two estimates disagree by tens of per cent and agree on the order of magnitude, which is the only part the lesson uses. Both are constructions for a reference body rather than measurements of any person, both depend on assumptions about which cell types dominate the count, and the bacterial figure is derived from a density per gram of stool and an assumed colon volume.
